claim: Obesity affects approximately 13% of the world's adult population.
source: Obesity has become a global health problem, affecting approximately 13% of the world's adult population, and over 340 million children and adolescents (WHO).
evidence: Cited from WHO source

claim: Obesity affects over 340 million children and adolescents.
source: Obesity has become a global health problem, affecting approximately 13% of the world's adult population, and over 340 million children and adolescents (WHO).
evidence: Cited from WHO source

claim: Maternal obesity reduces the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that maternal obesity reduces the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis (Chen et al., 2022b), deteriorates oocyte cytoplasmic quality and nuclear maturation, and disrupts genome methylation (Broughton and Moley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2022b

claim: Maternal obesity deteriorates oocyte cytoplasmic quality and nuclear maturation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that maternal obesity reduces the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis (Chen et al., 2022b), deteriorates oocyte cytoplasmic quality and nuclear maturation, and disrupts genome methylation (Broughton and Moley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broughton and Moley, 2017

claim: Maternal obesity disrupts genome methylation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that maternal obesity reduces the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis (Chen et al., 2022b), deteriorates oocyte cytoplasmic quality and nuclear maturation, and disrupts genome methylation (Broughton and Moley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broughton and Moley, 2017

claim: Reduced expression of Stella in oocytes induced by obesity results in global hypo-methylation in zygotes.
source: Reduced expression of Stella in oocytes induced by obesity results in global hypo-methylation in zygotes, which has an important contribution to the defective embryo development (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2018

claim: Global hypo-methylation in zygotes has an important contribution to defective embryo development.
source: Reduced expression of Stella in oocytes induced by obesity results in global hypo-methylation in zygotes, which has an important contribution to the defective embryo development (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2018

claim: Progeny of obese females has a higher risk of non-communicable diseases, such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases.
source: Furthermore, progeny of obese females has a higher risk of non-communicable diseases, such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases (Godfrey et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Godfrey et al., 2017

claim: Leptin is secreted from fat cells and associated with energy metabolism and obesity.
source: Leptin is secreted from fat cells and associated with energy metabolism and obesity (Obradovic et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Obradovic et al., 2021

claim: Obesity altered the methylation status of Leptin, which might play a role in the metabolic disorders of female offspring.
source: Our previous study indicated that obesity altered the methylation status of Leptin, which might play a role in the metabolic disorders of female offspring.
evidence: Authors' previous study

claim: Methylation changes in Leptin are not detected in the first-generation (F1) oocytes.
source: However, these methylation changes are not detected in the first-generation (F1) oocytes (Ge et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ge et al., 2014

claim: Elevated levels of circulating free fatty acids in obese females contribute to oocyte lipotoxicity.
source: Elevated levels of circulating free fatty acids in obese females contribute to oocyte lipotoxicity, while concomitantly diminishing mitochondrial function within oocytes (Broughton and Moley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broughton and Moley, 2017

claim: Elevated levels of circulating free fatty acids in obese females diminish mitochondrial function within oocytes.
source: Elevated levels of circulating free fatty acids in obese females contribute to oocyte lipotoxicity, while concomitantly diminishing mitochondrial function within oocytes (Broughton and Moley, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broughton and Moley, 2017

claim: Decreased melatonin levels are reported in animals and humans.
source: The decreased melatonin levels are also reported in animals and humans by previous studies (Overberg et al., 2022; Virto et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Overberg et al., 2022 and Virto et al., 2018

claim: Melatonin has contributions to metabolism and DNA methylation in somatic cells.
source: Melatonin has contributions to metabolism and DNA methylation in somatic cells (Davoodvandi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davoodvandi et al., 2022

claim: The HFD group exhibited a significantly higher average body weight compared to the CD group.
source: The HFD group exhibited a significantly higher average body weight compared to the CD group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Re-methylation in oocytes occurs in follicular development and is nearly complete at the germinal vesicle (GV) stage.
source: Re-methylation in oocytes occurs in follicular development and is nearly complete at the germinal vesicle (GV) stage.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The 5mC and 5hmC levels in the GV oocytes of HFD mice were significantly higher than that in the CD group.
source: The 5mC (5-methylcytosine) and 5hmC (5-hydroxymethylcytosine) levels in the GV oocytes of HFD mice were significantly higher than that in the CD group (Figure 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: Global methylation in MII oocytes of the HFD group was higher than that in the CD group.
source: We found that global methylation in MII oocytes of the HFD group was higher than that in the CD group (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The CG methylation level in MII oocytes of HFD was significantly higher than that in the CD group.
source: We found that the CG methylation level in MII oocytes of HFD was significantly higher than that in the CD group (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Differentially methylated CG is distributed across all chromosomes.
source: Differentially methylated CG is distributed across all chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Hyper-methylation was distributed in the promoter, exon, upstream 2 k, and downstream 2 k regions of genes in HFD oocytes.
source: Results showed that the hyper-methylation was distributed in the promoter, exon, upstream 2 k, and downstream 2 k regions (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) of genes in HFD oocytes.
evidence: Supported by methylation distribution analysis shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Maternal obesity results in hyper-genome methylation in oocytes.
source: These findings suggest that maternal obesity results in hyper-genome methylation in oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the methylation data presented

claim: 4340 DMRs were identified between HFD and CD oocytes.
source: We further analyzed the DMRs in oocytes, and identified 4340 DMRs between HFD and CD oocytes.
evidence: Based on analysis of sequencing data

claim: Among the DMRs, 2013 were hyper-DMRs (46.38%), and 2327 were hypo-DMRs (53.62%).
source: Among these, 2013 were hyper-DMRs (46.38%), and 2327 were hypo-DMRs (53.62%) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 1G

claim: DMRs were distributed across all chromosomes.
source: These DMRs were distributed across all chromosomes (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H

claim: The hypo-DMRs were enriched in the UTR3, repeat, and intron regions compared with hyper-DMRs.
source: However, the hypo-DMRs were enriched in the UTR3, repeat, and intron regions compared with hyper-DMRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Genes with DMRs at promoters were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways including amino acid metabolism pathways, carbohydrate metabolism pathways, lipid metabolism pathways, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins pathways.
source: Results indicated that the genes with DMRs at promoters were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways including amino acid metabolism pathways, carbohydrate metabolism pathways, lipid metabolism pathways, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins pathways (Figure 1I, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1I and Supplementary file 2

claim: A total of 35 genes with DMRs at promoters were included in metabolism pathways, 19 of these genes were with hyper-DMRs and 16 of these genes were with hypo-DMRs.
source: A total of 35 genes with DMRs at promoters were included in metabolism pathways, 19 of these genes were with hyper-DMRs and 16 of these genes were with hypo-DMRs (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 3

claim: The altered methylation in oocytes induced by maternal obesity may play a role in the metabolic disorders in offspring.
source: These results suggest that the altered methylation in oocytes induced by maternal obesity may play a role in the metabolic disorders in offspring.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment of DMRs in metabolic pathways

claim: Disturbed methylation in oocytes caused by uterine undernourishment can be partly transmitted to F2 oocytes via females.
source: Our recent study demonstrated that disturbed methylation in oocytes caused by uterine undernourishment can be partly transmitted to F2 oocytes via females, which may play a key role in the transgenerational inheritance of metabolic disorders (Tang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2023

claim: The GTTs and ITTs of F0, F1, and F2 females were impaired.
source: We examined the glucose and insulin tolerance (GTT and ITT), and found that the GTTs and ITTs of F0, F1, and F2 females were impaired (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by GTT and ITT data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: The methylation levels of hyper-DMRs including Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR in HFD oocytes were significantly higher than in the CD group.
source: We found that the methylation levels of hyper-DMRs including Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR in HFD oocytes were significantly higher than in the CD group (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The methylation level of hypo-DMRs, Pik3cd-DMR in HFD oocytes was significantly lower than that in the CD group.
source: The methylation level of hypo-DMRs, Pik3cd-DMR in HFD oocytes was significantly lower than that in the CD group (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The methylation level of H19 was low in both HFD and CD oocytes.
source: To exclude the effects of somatic cell contamination, we examined the methylation level of paternally imprinted gene H19, which was low in both HFD and CD oocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The samples are not contaminated by somatic cells.
source: These findings indicate that the samples are not contaminated by somatic cells.
evidence: Inferred from low H19 methylation in oocytes

claim: The methylation levels of Bhlha15-DMR and Mgat1-DMR were higher and the methylation level of Pik3cd-DMR was lower in HF1 livers than that in CF1 livers.
source: Results revealed that the methylation levels of Bhlha15-DMR and Mgat1-DMR were higher and the methylation level of Pik3cd-DMR was lower in HF1 livers than that in CF1 livers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C

claim: The expression levels of Bhlha15, Mgat1, and Pdpk1 were significantly lower in HF1 livers compared to that in CF1.
source: The expression levels of Bhlha15, Mgat1, and Pdpk1 were significantly lower and the expression levels of Map3k8, Tkt, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF1 livers compared to that in CF1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F

claim: The expression levels of Map3k8, Tkt, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF1 livers compared to that in CF1.
source: The expression levels of Bhlha15, Mgat1, and Pdpk1 were significantly lower and the expression levels of Map3k8, Tkt, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF1 livers compared to that in CF1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F

claim: Mgat1 is associated with lipid metabolism and obesity.
source: Mgat1 is associated with lipid metabolism and obesity (Jacobsson et al., 2012; Johansson et al., 2010), Tkt regulates glucose metabolism (Bartáková et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2018), and Pik3cd is involved in lipid metabolism and diabetes (Hood et al., 2019; Wójcik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacobsson et al., 2012 and Johansson et al., 2010

claim: Tkt regulates glucose metabolism.
source: Mgat1 is associated with lipid metabolism and obesity (Jacobsson et al., 2012; Johansson et al., 2010), Tkt regulates glucose metabolism (Bartáková et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2018), and Pik3cd is involved in lipid metabolism and diabetes (Hood et al., 2019; Wójcik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartáková et al., 2016 and Kang et al., 2018

claim: Pik3cd is involved in lipid metabolism and diabetes.
source: Mgat1 is associated with lipid metabolism and obesity (Jacobsson et al., 2012; Johansson et al., 2010), Tkt regulates glucose metabolism (Bartáková et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2018), and Pik3cd is involved in lipid metabolism and diabetes (Hood et al., 2019; Wójcik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hood et al., 2019 and Wójcik et al., 2014

claim: The altered methylation in HFD oocytes is partly transmitted to F1 livers via oocytes.
source: These results suggest that the altered methylation in HFD oocytes is partly transmitted to F1 livers via oocytes, and that the abnormal methylation may be a reason for the disturbed metabolism of HF1.
evidence: Inferred from methylation and expression data in F1 livers

claim: Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR were significantly hyper-methylated in HF1 oocytes compared with CF1 oocytes.
source: Therefore, we examined the methylation of DMRs in F1 oocytes, and results revealed that Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR were significantly hyper-methylated in HF1 oocytes compared with CF1 oocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2E

claim: At least a part of the altered methylation in HFD oocytes is transmitted to F1 oocytes via females.
source: These results indicate that at least a part of the altered methylation in HFD oocytes is transmitted to F1 oocytes via females.
evidence: Inferred from methylation data in F1 oocytes

claim: The methylation of Bhlha15-DMR and Mgat1-DMR was higher and the methylation level of Pik3cd-DMR was lower in HF2 livers than that in CF2 livers.
source: The methylation of Bhlha15-DMR and Mgat1-DMR was higher and the methylation level of Pik3cd-DMR was lower in HF2 livers than that in CF2 livers (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C

claim: The expression levels of Bhlha15, Pdpk1, and Mgat1 were significantly lower in HF2 livers than that in CF2.
source: In addition, the expression levels of Bhlha15, Pdpk1, and Mgat1 were significantly lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E), and the expression levels of Pld1, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF2 livers than that in CF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E

claim: The expression levels of Pld1, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF2 livers than that in CF2.
source: In addition, the expression levels of Bhlha15, Pdpk1, and Mgat1 were significantly lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E), and the expression levels of Pld1, Pik3cd, and Sphk2 were significantly higher in HF2 livers than that in CF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F

claim: At least a part of the altered methylation in HF2 livers may be inherited from HFD oocytes.
source: These results suggest that at least a part of the altered methylation in HF2 livers may be inherited from HFD oocytes, and that this alteration may be associated with the disrupted metabolism in F2 offspring.
evidence: Inferred from methylation and expression data in F2 livers

claim: The hyper-methylation of Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR, and the hypo-methylation of Pik3cd-DMR and Tkt-DMR were maintained in HF2 oocytes.
source: We then examined the methylation of DMRs in F2 oocytes using BS, and found that the hyper-methylation of Bhlha15-DMR, Mgat1-DMR, and Taok3-DMR, and the hypo-methylation of Pik3cd-DMR and Tkt-DMR were maintained in HF2 oocytes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The methylation of Bhlha15-DMR was maintained from HFD oocytes to HF2 oocytes.
source: For hyper-DMRs, the methylation of Bhlha15-DMR was maintained from HFD oocytes to HF2 oocytes.
evidence: Based on analysis of methylation data across generations

claim: The methylation levels of Mgat1-DMR and Taok3-DMR were partly transmitted to HF2 oocytes.
source: Compared to those in HFD oocytes, the methylation levels of Mgat1-DMR and Taok3-DMR were partly transmitted to HF2 oocytes.
evidence: Based on analysis of methylation data across generations

claim: The methylation levels of Tkt-DMR and Pik3cd-DMR in HFD oocytes were inherited by HF2.
source: For hypo-DMRs, the methylation levels of Tkt-DMR and Pik3cd-DMR in HFD oocytes were inherited by HF2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Only a part of the altered methylation in HFD oocytes can be transmitted to F2 oocytes.
source: These results suggest that only a part of the altered methylation in HFD oocytes can be transmitted to F2 oocytes, and that disrupted methylation may be a reason for the inheritance of the metabolic disorders in F1 and F2.
evidence: Inferred from methylation data across generations

claim: Disrupted methylation may be a reason for the inheritance of the metabolic disorders in F1 and F2.
source: These results suggest that only a part of the altered methylation in HFD oocytes can be transmitted to F2 oocytes, and that disrupted methylation may be a reason for the inheritance of the metabolic disorders in F1 and F2.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between methylation changes and metabolic phenotypes

claim: The PC1 and PC2 explained 44.6% and 9.96% of the total metabolite variation, respectively.
source: The principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the PC1 and PC2, respectively, explained 44.6% and 9.96% of the total metabolite variation, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The distribution of extracts between groups was distinguishable.
source: The distribution of extracts between groups was distinguishable (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by PCA shown in Figure 3A

claim: 538 differential metabolites were identified, including 288 upregulated and 250 downregulated metabolites.
source: We identified 538 differential metabolites based on the PLS-DA (robust orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis) and T-test analysis with the following criteria: VIP (variable importance in projection) ≥1, fold change ≥1.2 or≤0.83, and P-value <0.05, including 288 upregulated and 250 downregulated metabolites (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Differential metabolites were significantly enriched in tryptophan and vitamin B6 metabolism.
source: The enrichment of differential metabolites was analyzed using KEGG, which revealed that differential metabolites were significantly enriched in tryptophan and vitamin B6 metabolism (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Obesity disturbs the metabolomics of serum.
source: These results suggest that obesity disturbs the metabolomics of serum.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data

claim: The concentration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group.
source: The concentration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), L-methionine, and L-tyrosine was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D-G

claim: The concentration of L-methionine was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group.
source: The concentration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), L-methionine, and L-tyrosine was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D-G

claim: The concentration of L-tyrosine was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group.
source: The concentration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), L-methionine, and L-tyrosine was significantly increased in HFD serum compared with the CD group (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D-G

claim: During the DNA methylation process, the methyl group donor S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is degraded into S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) and homocysteine (HCY).
source: During the DNA methylation process, the methyl group donor S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is degraded into S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) and homocysteine (HCY) (Chen et al., 2004), and vitamin B6 serves as a co-factor (Vaccaro and Naser, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2004

claim: Vitamin B6 serves as a co-factor in DNA methylation.
source: During the DNA methylation process, the methyl group donor S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is degraded into S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) and homocysteine (HCY) (Chen et al., 2004), and vitamin B6 serves as a co-factor (Vaccaro and Naser, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaccaro and Naser, 2021

claim: Excessive methionine and vitamin B6 intake results in hyper-methylation.
source: Excessive methionine and vitamin B6 intake results in hyper-methylation (Waterland, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waterland, 2006

claim: The concentrations of SAM, SAH, and HCY in HFD livers were similar to those in CD livers.
source: Results showed that the concentrations of SAM, SAH, and HCY in HFD livers were similar to those in CD livers (Figure 3H–J), and the concentration of SAM in HFD oocytes was lower than that in the CD group (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H-J

claim: The concentration of SAM in HFD oocytes was lower than that in the CD group.
source: Results showed that the concentrations of SAM, SAH, and HCY in HFD livers were similar to those in CD livers (Figure 3H–J), and the concentration of SAM in HFD oocytes was lower than that in the CD group (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3K

claim: The higher concentrations of methionine and pyridoxine in the serum of HFD mice may not be the main reason for the genomic hyper-methylation in oocytes.
source: These results suggest that the higher concentrations of methionine and pyridoxine in the serum of HFD mice may not be the main reason for the genomic hyper-methylation in oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from SAM, SAH, and HCY measurements

claim: The concentrations of genistein and dibutylpthalate were similar between HFD and CD serum.
source: The results revealed that the concentrations of these metabolites were similar between HFD and CD serum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which suggests that these metabolites may have no effect on the altered methylation in oocytes.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The concentration of melatonin in the HFD serum was significantly lower than that in the CD group.
source: As presented in Figure 3D and L, the concentration of melatonin in the HFD serum was significantly lower than that in the CD group.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D and L

claim: Low concentrations of melatonin have been reported in obese rats.
source: Low concentrations of melatonin have also been reported in obese rats (Virto et al., 2018) and humans (Overberg et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Virto et al., 2018

claim: Low concentrations of melatonin have been reported in obese humans.
source: Low concentrations of melatonin have also been reported in obese rats (Virto et al., 2018) and humans (Overberg et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Overberg et al., 2022

claim: Melatonin affects DNA re-methylation in oocytes.
source: Melatonin affects DNA re-methylation in oocytes (Lan et al., 2018; Saeedabadi et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lan et al., 2018; Saeedabadi et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2019

claim: Exogenous melatonin treatment significantly reduced the hyper-methylation of HFD oocytes.
source: Here, we found that if HFD mice were treated with exogenous melatonin for 14 d, the genomic hyper-methylation in HFD oocytes was significantly reduced (Figure 3M and N).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3M and N

claim: The reduced melatonin concentration may be involved in regulating the hyper-methylation of HFD oocytes.
source: These results suggest that the reduced melatonin concentration may be involved in regulating the hyper-methylation of HFD oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from melatonin treatment effects

claim: Melatonin receptors (MT1 and 2), which are coupled with inhibitor G-protein (Gi), have been identified in oocytes and granulosa cells.
source: Melatonin receptors (MT1 and 2), which are coupled with inhibitor G-protein (Gi), have been identified in oocytes and granulosa cells (Jin et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin et al., 2022 and Wang et al., 2021

claim: Activated Gi inhibits the activation of adenylyl cyclases (ADCYs), resulting in a decrease of cAMP.
source: Activated Gi inhibits the activation of adenylyl cyclases (ADCYs), resulting in a decrease of cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate), which regulates the activation of protein kinase A (PKA) and CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) (Wongprayoon and Govitrapong, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wongprayoon and Govitrapong, 2021

claim: Elevated cAMP level increases the expression of DNMTs resulting in hyper-methylation in HL-1 cardiomyocytes.
source: Elevated cAMP level increases the expression of DNMTs resulting in hyper-methylation in HL-1 cardiomyocytes (Fang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fang et al., 2015

claim: Luzindole treatment significantly increased the global methylation of 5mC and 5hmC in oocytes.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, female C57BL/6 mice fed with a normal diet were treated with luzindole, an inhibitor of melatonin receptor, and the global methylation of 5mC and 5hmC was significantly increased in oocytes (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: Luzindole did not affect the concentration of melatonin in the serum.
source: Luzindole did not affect the concentration of melatonin in the serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Excessive melatonin treatment significantly increased the concentration of melatonin in the serum.
source: However, excessive melatonin treatment significantly increased the concentration of melatonin in the serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and decreased the methylation levels of 5mC and 5hmC in oocytes (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Excessive melatonin treatment decreased the methylation levels of 5mC and 5hmC in oocytes.
source: However, excessive melatonin treatment significantly increased the concentration of melatonin in the serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and decreased the methylation levels of 5mC and 5hmC in oocytes (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: Melatonin may regulate the re-methylation process in oocytes.
source: These findings indicate that melatonin may regulate the re-methylation process in oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from luzindole and melatonin treatment effects

claim: ADCY5, 6, and 9 were expressed in oocytes.
source: To confirm whether melatonin regulates methylation in oocytes via the cAMP pathway, we examined the expression of ADCYs in oocytes using RT-PCR, and found that ADCY5, 6, and 9 were expressed in oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The melatonin antagonist luzindole significantly increased the expression of ADCY6 and ADCY9 in oocytes.
source: The melatonin antagonist luzindole significantly increased the expression of ADCY6 and ADCY9 in oocytes, and melatonin reduced the expression of ADCY6 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Melatonin reduced the expression of ADCY6.
source: The melatonin antagonist luzindole significantly increased the expression of ADCY6 and ADCY9 in oocytes, and melatonin reduced the expression of ADCY6 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The melatonin antagonist luzindole increased the concentration of cAMP in oocytes.
source: In addition, the melatonin antagonist luzindole increased, while melatonin decreased the concentration of cAMP in oocytes, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Melatonin decreased the concentration of cAMP in oocytes.
source: In addition, the melatonin antagonist luzindole increased, while melatonin decreased the concentration of cAMP in oocytes, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Melatonin may regulate the synthesis of cAMP via ADCY6 in oocytes.
source: These results suggest that melatonin may regulate the synthesis of cAMP via ADCY6 in oocytes.
evidence: Inferred from ADCY expression and cAMP concentration data

claim: SQ22536 treatment significantly reduced the global methylation of 5mC and the concentration of cAMP in oocytes.
source: To further confirm the role of cAMP in regulating the methylation of oocytes, we treated mice with SQ22536, an inhibitor of ADCYs, and found that this treatment significantly reduced the global methylation of 5mC and the concentration of cAMP in oocytes (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and ELISA data shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: The ADCYs activator forskolin significantly increased the cAMP concentration and global methylation of 5mC in oocytes.
source: Whereas, the ADCYs activator forskolin significantly increased the cAMP concentration and global methylation of 5mC in oocytes (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and ELISA data shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: 8-Bromo-cAMP increased the global methylation in oocytes.
source: 8-Bromo-cAMP, a cAMP analogue, also increased the global methylation in oocytes (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: H89 2HCL treatment significantly reduced the global methylation of 5mC in oocytes.
source: When we treated mice with H89 2HCL, a PKA antagonist, the global methylation of 5mC was significantly reduced in oocytes (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: Melatonin may mediate DNA methylation in oocytes via the cAMP/PKA pathway.
source: These results suggest that melatonin may mediate DNA methylation in oocytes via the cAMP/PKA pathway.
